releases.theme: the templates directory becomes a directory — every one of the twenty-seven relationship templates gets a public page, and My Templates lists only the templates a member actually owns.
releases.headline: `feat(templates)` — every template has a page, not just a card (#782) (#782)

releases.theme: the payment decision moves into the stage that asks for it, and the create saves a draft that pays when its opinions publish.
releases.headline: `feat(flow)` — stage 4 walks the payment in place, and the create is a draft that pays at publish (#771)

releases.theme: the build draws what the review approved — the create flow's panel stops at 880px, one stage foot carries [Back][Cancel] and the advance, Settings asks its two questions side by side, and an Aspect row reads 01 · grip · name · opinions · edit.
releases.headline: `feat(flow)` — the build matches the v7 artifact — shell width, footers, Settings peers, Aspect rows (#760) (#761)

releases.theme: the capture moves into a frame — Stripe's form mounts inside the dialog, so paying never leaves the relationship, while the membership checkout stays hosted.
releases.headline: `feat(payment)` — the capture is an embedded form in the dialog, not a hosted link (#748) (#751)

releases.theme: the payer can pay — a method is captured and a relationship completes, an invited counterparty answers inside the same modal, templates publish revisions instead of being destroyed, and paying still opens Stripe's own page rather than a frame.
releases.headline: `feat(crud)` — templates publish revisions and are retired, never destroyed in use (#711) (#742)

releases.theme: the flow conforms to its six-stage spec — Details · Settings · Aspects · Invite · Connect · Align — opens as one modal, and no action form asks for a Reason.
releases.headline: `feat(flow)` — conform to the six-stage spec — Details · Settings · Aspects · Invite · Connect · Align (#735) (#737)

releases.theme: the review shelf goes live — every prototype grouped by the release it ships with, with the approved six-stage flow as its first artifact.
releases.headline: `feat(admin)` — the /admin/review shelf: the review store, the release-grouped list and the writes, with the six-stage prototype as its v5 artifact (#670) (#673) (#677)

releases.theme: pay-to-complete: the fee moves from creation to completion, and the member rail stops asking three shelves apart.
releases.headline: `feat(billing)` — pay-to-complete: the counterparty submits, the initiator picks a plan and pays, and the Gap opens (#619)

releases.theme: the gate notices when its own evidence has aged, and the screens a real flow needed get a door.
releases.headline: `fix(health)` — a stale platform-health record fails the gate instead of rendering as current (#599)

releases.theme: account deletion a person can perform themselves, with the intent recorded before anything is destroyed.
releases.headline: `feat(privacy)` — account deletion: 0033 indexes, the auth-user delete, one transactional scrub, an in-app control (#597)

releases.theme: the operator's console — one audited write path — and relationship templates become products a member can own.
releases.headline: an audited operations console: every write passes `act()`, every action carries a reason, and `product.admin` is a capability (#500)

releases.theme: the two-party flow closes — create, answer blind, accept, and the Gap opens on the second acceptance.
releases.headline: `feat(flow)` — acceptance is the completion hinge, and Steps are derived on the transition (#427)

releases.theme: five read surfaces go live from Postgres, and every write surface says on screen that it cannot write.
releases.headline: five read surfaces server-rendered from the database — relationships, their sessions, the template catalogue and the report (#412)

releases.theme: the template becomes a product: a brand record, a parity gate, and the two-party assessment flow on six tables.
releases.headline: `feat(db)` — six content tables, the database-backed assessment screen, and the db scripts (#145)

releases.theme: one record type, two brands and no database — the webapp stops being a mock of a business nobody ran.
releases.headline: `feat(content)` — one record type, two templates: a quiz and an assessment (#128)
